international.title: Tories welcome Louise Haigh’s hint government could adopt their plan to scrap Natural England – UK politics live
international.summary: First secretary of state has declined to say whether Natural England will be abolished as part of plans to cut the number of quangos Natural England could be abolished as part of quango cull, says Louise Haigh Rain Newton-Smith , the CBI chief executive, opened the organisation’s conference in London this morning with some relatively positive comments about the PM. Here are extracts from what she said. Newton-Smith praised Burnham for bringing “hope” back to politics. She said: In the last few years, we in the UK have been too ready to talk ourselves down. To put on our gloom-tinted glasses. They don’t sit well on me. The prime minister has brought a dose of hope to our politics. And just as pessimism can be self-fulfilling, confidence can be contagious. It’s time we gave a shot of confidence to our economy. It’s time we got serious about a brighter future for our children. She said the government needed to reassure business that “public control” of utilities did not mean nationalisation. On investment … to some, “public control” sounds like code for renationalisation. That is kryptonite to investment. We know that’s not what’s coming – but give us the reassurance we need. Show this is a model built on partnership, not primacy. That government wants private capital at the table – not heading for the exit. She said Burnham was right to start a debate about a closer relationship with the EU. The prime minister is right to have this conversation. Brexit was a wrong turn for our economy. It gave us greater sovereignty. But sovereignty without prosperity is not enough. We didn’t vote to be poorer. This is no time to re-fight the referendum. But we must come back to the table with bolder ambition. She said that regional devolution could unlock investment and that the CBI was involved in a scheme to help give mayoral authorities more financial expertise. There is promise in devolution. Done right, it can give business one front door for decisions that unlock investment. Done wrong, it could fracture confidence… leave regions competing with each other when they should be competing with the world. The difference is whether authorities have the capacity and skills. Today, I can announce the CBI and our members are partnering with the National Wealth Fund and mayoral authorities across the UK … to parachute in senior financial secondees with the experience to make investment happen. The Times has been told that proposals for greater public control, due to be announced next month in Burnham’s ten-year plan for government, will include cuts to the arms-length bodies Haigh blames for planning delays, pollution and high energy costs. Natural England, the environment regulator, could be among the casualties. Senior ministers believe it is obstructing government plans to build hundreds of thousands of homes, piling unnecessary costs onto developers and preventing the construction of infrastructure. We’re considering all arms-length bodies, both devolving, dissolving, and bringing back into departments because we cannot continue with this situation where politicians look round and can’t take responsibility for the actions that people have elected their government for. For far too long, Natural England has been allowed to hold the country to ransom, blocking desperately needed homes and vital infrastructure. That’s why the Conservatives have pledged to abolish it. Now, it seems Labour are lifting that plan wholesale. Continue reading...
